concepts.name: Price Elasticity of Demand (PED): Measurement and Interpretation
key_dimensions: Formula: % change in quantity demanded / % change in price and its sign convention (always negative, why absolute value is used)
Interpretation of coefficient values: perfectly inelastic (0), inelastic (<1), unitary (=1), elastic (>1), perfectly elastic (infinity)
UPSC trap: distinguishing between 'elasticity' (ratio) vs 'slope' of demand curve — a common confusion point
Geometric method of measuring PED at a point on a linear demand curve

concepts.name: Determinants of Price Elasticity of Demand
key_dimensions: Nature of the good: necessities vs luxuries and their typical elasticity ranges
Availability of substitutes: more substitutes = more elastic (e.g., branded goods vs generic)
Time horizon: demand becomes more elastic over longer periods (consumer adjustment)
Proportion of income spent: expensive goods (car) tend to be more elastic than cheap goods (salt)
UPSC trap: habit-forming goods (tobacco, alcohol) are inelastic despite being 'non-necessities'

concepts.name: Relationship Between PED, Total Revenue, and Tax Incidence
key_dimensions: TR test: elastic demand → price rise reduces TR; inelastic demand → price rise increases TR; unitary → TR unchanged
Policy relevance: government taxes inelastic goods (fuel, tobacco) to maximize revenue with minimal quantity reduction
Tax burden shifting: with inelastic demand, consumers bear more of the tax burden regardless of who is legally taxed
UPSC trap: confusing 'tax incidence' (economic burden) with 'tax impact' (legal liability)

concepts.name: Cross Price Elasticity of Demand (XED): Substitutes vs Complements
key_dimensions: Formula and sign interpretation: positive XED = substitutes (tea & coffee), negative XED = complements (car & petrol)
Magnitude of XED: close substitutes have high positive XED; weak complements have small negative XED
Policy application: anti-trust/competition policy uses XED to define market boundaries
UPSC trap: zero or near-zero XED does NOT necessarily mean unrelated goods — could be independent goods

concepts.name: Income Elasticity of Demand (YED): Normal, Inferior, and Giffen Goods
key_dimensions: Sign convention: positive YED = normal good; negative YED = inferior good
Magnitude within normal goods: YED between 0 and 1 = necessity; YED > 1 = luxury good
Engel's Law: as income rises, proportion spent on food falls — implies food has YED < 1
UPSC trap: Giffen goods have negative PED (not just negative YED) — must not conflate Giffen with inferior goods; all Giffen are inferior but not all inferior are Giffen

concepts.name: Giffen Goods and the Giffen Paradox
key_dimensions: Definition: goods where demand rises when price rises — violating the law of demand (positive PED)
Mechanism: strong negative income effect overwhelms the substitution effect for inferior goods consumed in large quantities
Classic examples: staple foods (coarse grains) among very poor households in developing countries
UPSC trap: Giffen goods are NOT the same as Veblen goods — Giffen is driven by income effect among poor; Veblen is driven by prestige/snob effect among rich

concepts.name: Veblen Goods and Conspicuous Consumption
key_dimensions: Definition: luxury/prestige goods where demand increases with price due to status signaling (positive PED)
Distinction from normal goods: utility derived partly from high price itself (Rolex, luxury cars)
UPSC trap: Veblen goods appear to violate law of demand but the mechanism is different from Giffen goods — must specify which and why
Policy implication: imposing luxury tax may paradoxically increase their desirability

concepts.name: Price Elasticity of Supply (PES): Measurement and Determinants
key_dimensions: Formula: % change in quantity supplied / % change in price; always positive (upward sloping supply)
Key determinants: time period (momentary vs short run vs long run), availability of inputs, production flexibility, spare capacity
UPSC trap: PES of perishable goods is near zero in the very short run (supply cannot be stored or increased quickly) but rises over time
Agricultural goods: inelastic in short run due to crop cycles; industrial goods: more elastic due to scalable production

concepts.name: Time Horizons and Elasticity of Supply: Market Period, Short Run, Long Run
key_dimensions: Market period (momentary): supply is perfectly inelastic — quantity is fixed (fish caught today)
Short run: some inputs fixed, supply partially elastic — can increase output by working existing capacity harder
Long run: all inputs variable, supply most elastic — new firms enter, full capacity adjustment possible
UPSC trap: 'short run' and 'long run' are NOT fixed time durations — they are defined by the fixity of factors, not calendar time

concepts.name: Perfectly Elastic and Perfectly Inelastic Demand/Supply: Graphical and Policy Implications
key_dimensions: Perfectly inelastic demand (vertical curve, PED=0): essential medicines, insulin — quantity unchanged regardless of price
Perfectly elastic demand (horizontal curve, PED=∞): perfectly competitive firm's demand curve — price taker
Perfectly inelastic supply (vertical): fixed supply goods like land, vintage art, spectrum in short run
UPSC trap: a horizontal supply curve (perfectly elastic supply) implies constant cost industry — not zero elasticity

concepts.name: Elasticity and the Burden of Indirect Taxes (Tax Incidence Analysis)
key_dimensions: When demand is more inelastic than supply: consumers bear greater tax burden
When supply is more inelastic than demand: producers bear greater tax burden
Extreme cases: perfectly inelastic demand = entire burden on consumer; perfectly inelastic supply = entire burden on producer
UPSC application: GST on essential goods vs luxury goods — differential incidence; rationale for exempting food and medicine

concepts.name: Price Floors, Price Ceilings, and Elasticity Interactions
key_dimensions: Price ceiling below equilibrium: shortage; severity of shortage depends on elasticity of demand and supply
Price floor above equilibrium: surplus; size of surplus depends on elasticity
MSP (Minimum Support Price) in India as a price floor: elastic supply means large surplus procurement burden on FCI
UPSC trap: price ceiling reduces quantity supplied — impact on consumers depends on whether demand is elastic or inelastic

concepts.name: Elasticity and Agricultural Markets: Special Characteristics
key_dimensions: Agricultural supply is price inelastic in short run due to biological production lags (crop cycle)
Cobweb theorem / price instability: inelastic supply + volatile demand causes cyclical price swings in agriculture
Income inelasticity of demand for food (Engel's Law): rising incomes benefit agriculture less proportionately
UPSC policy link: why price supports, buffer stocks, and MSP are needed — market failures due to inelasticity

concepts.name: Elasticity of Demand for Labour and Wages
key_dimensions: Derived demand: labour demand elasticity depends on elasticity of demand for the final product
Hicks-Marshall rules: labour demand more inelastic when — product demand inelastic, labour hard to substitute, labour cost is small share of total cost, supply of substitutes is inelastic
UPSC relevance: minimum wage debates — if labour demand is inelastic, minimum wage causes less unemployment
Gig economy: elastic labour demand due to easy substitutability with technology/automation

concepts.name: Advertisement/Promotional Elasticity of Demand
key_dimensions: Definition: % change in demand / % change in advertising expenditure
Higher for new products, competitive markets, and branded goods with close substitutes
Distinction from PED: captures non-price demand determinants; important in monopolistic competition
UPSC trap: high advertising elasticity does NOT mean high price elasticity — they measure different demand drivers

concepts.name: Elasticity and Subsidy Policy: Effectiveness and Leakage
key_dimensions: Consumer subsidy effectiveness: greater benefit to consumers when demand is elastic (they buy significantly more)
Producer subsidy effectiveness: greater benefit to producers when supply is inelastic (they capture more of the subsidy as profit)
India context: fertilizer subsidy incidence — inelastic supply of urea means producers/retailers capture significant subsidy rent
UPSC trap: subsidy does NOT always benefit the intended recipient — incidence depends on relative elasticities, not who receives the subsidy legally

concepts.name: Unitary Elasticity: Special Properties and Rectangular Hyperbola
key_dimensions: Demand curve with unitary elasticity (PED = -1) throughout is a rectangular hyperbola (P × Q = constant)
TR remains constant at all price levels when PED = 1 — TR test application
UPSC trap: a straight-line demand curve does NOT have constant elasticity — elasticity changes at every point even if slope is constant
Midpoint (arc elasticity) formula: used to calculate elasticity between two points to avoid the 'which point' ambiguity

concepts.name: Elasticity vs Slope of Demand/Supply Curves: A Common UPSC Trap
key_dimensions: Slope = ΔP/ΔQ (or ΔQ/ΔP); Elasticity = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q) — elasticity incorporates the ratio P/Q unlike slope
Two parallel demand curves: same slope but different elasticity at the same price level (flatter does NOT always mean more elastic)
Along a single straight-line demand curve: elasticity falls continuously from ∞ (at y-intercept) to 0 (at x-intercept)
UPSC trap: 'steeper demand curve means more inelastic' is ONLY valid when comparing curves passing through the same point

concepts.name: Supply Elasticity of Key Indian Commodities and Policy Implications
key_dimensions: Land supply: perfectly inelastic in aggregate — entire rent is economic surplus (Ricardian rent concept link)
Urban housing supply elasticity: low in India due to FSI restrictions, land acquisition bottlenecks — drives housing inflation
Petroleum/fuel: inelastic supply in India (import dependent) — price volatility has large macroeconomic pass-through
UPSC link: OPEC production cuts → inelastic global oil demand → large price rise; India's fuel subsidy burden explanation

concepts.name: Elasticity Concepts in International Trade: Terms of Trade and Export/Import Policy
key_dimensions: Marshall-Lerner condition: depreciation improves trade balance ONLY if sum of absolute PED of exports and imports > 1
J-curve effect: in short run, trade balance worsens after depreciation (inelastic responses) before improving in long run
Export taxes on inelastic demand commodities (e.g., iron ore, rare earths) — government captures rent without large quantity loss
UPSC trap: a weak rupee does NOT automatically improve India's trade deficit if import demand (especially oil) is highly inelastic
